briefing.opening: Good morning/afternoon, everyone. I will now begin the climate briefing for October 4, 2026.

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Domestic Carbon Neutrality Efforts and Community Participation
sections.content: Today, various efforts by local governments and communities in South Korea to respond to the climate crisis were highlighted. Seongnam City's hosting of a Healthy City Symposium [1] and Yeonggwang County's creation of outdoor shelters for smart farm workers [2] present localized solutions. Gwacheon City held reporting sessions and a final report session for its local energy plan for carbon neutrality [4, 13], and Naju City achieved recognition as an excellent city/county for two consecutive years in the administrative sector for carbon neutrality practices [5]. Yeongcheon Saemaul Association, Yeoju City, and Cheonan Carbon Neutrality Support Center launched campaigns to spread a culture of carbon neutrality in festival venues and daily life [3, 7, 9, 11, 12, 14], and students at Gongju Geumhak Elementary School are learning about carbon neutrality through horticultural activities [8], demonstrating ongoing efforts in the educational sector. However, the 'Climate Crisis Emergency Action' group criticized that the amendment to the Carbon Neutrality Act does not adequately reflect the intent of the Constitutional Court's decision [6], raising the need for policy improvements.

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Expansion of Renewable Energy and Infrastructure Development
sections.content: In the domestic renewable energy sector, news of infrastructure expansion and technological development continued. Jeju Province has invested 35 billion won to commence the development of technology for storing surplus renewable energy as hydrogen [17], and Korea Western Power is accelerating the development of onshore and offshore wind power in the Gwangju-Jeonnam region in cooperation with Jeonnam Development Corporation [18]. Helper's Solution, a climate and energy welfare company, strengthened its cooperation by signing a business agreement with Geumsan ENG, a solar power specialist [16]. Meanwhile, challenges related to stably producing hydrogen using highly variable renewable energy were raised [20], and there was also a call for the Korea Meteorological Administration to implement a 'large-scale power outage risk weather' alert system in preparation for the era of renewable energy [15]. Amidst this, the growth potential of related industries is also drawing attention, with the lightning rod market [19] and cable management system market [23] projected to be driven by renewable energy and smart grids by 2035.

sections.title: 🌍 International Climate Change Legal Issues and Policy Trends
sections.content: Internationally, legal issues related to climate change are emerging as major agenda items. The U.S. Supreme Court is set to begin its new term by hearing major climate change cases [27, 31, 35, 36], and plans to hear attempts by energy companies to end Boulder's climate change lawsuit [25]. Notably, a lawsuit filed by Exxon is drawing attention for its potential to protect Houston's oil industry from climate change-related litigation [32]. The Supreme Court is reviewing the future of climate change lawsuits [37], which is expected to significantly impact the direction of climate policies for businesses and governments in the future. In addition, policy response efforts by the international community are continuing, such as in Bangladesh, where a JS parliamentary delegation held a meeting to discuss climate change and migration issues, encouraging active participation from members [52].

sections.title: 🔴 Increasing Global Climate Change Impacts and Threats
sections.content: Globally, the threat of climate change has become more visible, with its impacts reported across various sectors. The Pacific island nation of Tuvalu is on the front lines of climate change [38], and while Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, is adapting to floods, the threat of flooding has reportedly increased due to climate change [40]. Pakistan warned that climate change poses an existential threat to food security [43], and over 80% of trees in Luxembourg's forests are suffering, facing unprecedented decline [44]. The National Trust stated that climate threats to cultural heritage have become 'visible' through recent summers [53], and concerns were heightened by the revelation that the UK government quietly scrapped wildfire preparedness plans for rural England [54]. Furthermore, an analysis linking New Jersey's (N.J.) health crisis to climate change [33], along with reports that climate change is making some grocery prices more expensive this year [48], warns of impacts on daily life.

sections.title: 🌱 International Efforts and Awareness Raising for Climate Change Response
sections.content: Amidst these threats, international efforts and awareness-raising to respond to climate change continue. India is accelerating its energy transition by including 50 GWh of storage facilities in its renewable energy transmission grid [21]. Thailand is helping farmers prepare for climate change to protect food security [41], and maps are supporting conservation efforts by identifying potential areas where threatened Himalayan medicinal plants can survive amidst climate change [42]. In the education sector, positive changes are also emerging, such as over 1,200 students in Colorado earning climate 'certifications' [55], and learners becoming interested in climate change through energy challenges [51]. Furthermore, director Tom McCarthy's climate change drama-comedy film 'A Statement' subtly reflects the current climate change situation [29, 34], contributing to public awareness.

briefing.closing: Today's briefing has highlighted diverse response efforts both domestically and internationally amidst the climate crisis, alongside a simultaneous escalation of legal, policy, and environmental threats. It is a critical juncture where understanding the complex aspects of climate change and developing integrated countermeasures becomes even more crucial. This concludes today's climate briefing.
